intro: The Prélude is the first movement of Ravel’s memorial suite Le Tombeau de Couperin, and its line is carried in continuous rapid semiquavers. Isaac David plays the original version for piano.

sections.label: A · Semiquavers with ornaments, E minor
sections.mNote: Long held notes sound over quick E minor semiquaver figures.

sections.label: Dev · Running notes in the left hand
sections.mNote: Running notes pass beneath a more sustained right hand.

sections.label: B · The piano climbs
sections.mNote: The hands spread apart as the phrases grow.

sections.label: Coda · Falling runs and held notes
sections.mNote: Descending runs, then a held bass, then a final climb.

cues.title: Opening in E minor
cues.text: The piano begins in E minor, Vif, with twelve semiquavers to the bar. Longer notes are held across the running figures. Ravel specifies that the grace notes fall on the beat.
cues.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Prélude, opening and footnote on grace notes; also Piano Practical Editions, pp. 5–6. https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/48/IMSLP560971-PMLP4975-Le_Tombeau_de_Couperin.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dedication to Jacques Charlot
cues.text: Above the first notes stands the name of Lieutenant Jacques Charlot, Ravel’s friend and a cousin of his publisher Jacques Durand. Charlot was one of the friends killed in the First World War whose names Ravel gave to the suite’s movements.
cues.evidence: The dedication is recorded by the BnF: https://catalogue.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cb13917720k. Eric T. Williams identifies Charlot and the wartime dedications in the Kansas City Symphony programme, 5–7 April 2024, p. 6: https://www.kcsymphony.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/FY24-CS10-Program-Book-Digital-2024-04-05.pdf

cues.title: Letter on a French suite, 1914
cues.text: On 1 October 1914, after the war had begun, Ravel wrote to his former pupil about a French suite: “The Marseillaise doesn’t come into it at all, but there’ll be a forlane and a jig.”
cues.evidence: Ravel to Roland-Manuel, 1 October 1914, quoted by Eric T. Williams, Kansas City Symphony programme, 5–7 April 2024, p. 5. https://www.kcsymphony.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/FY24-CS10-Program-Book-Digital-2024-04-05.pdf

cues.title: Semiquavers in the left hand
cues.text: The left hand takes over the semiquavers while the right hand holds its line above them. Ravel moves the semiquavers down into the bass, then back across the keyboard. The hands continue to exchange the running semiquavers and the sustained line.
cues.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Prélude, pp. 4–5; Piano Practical Editions, bars 40–75, shows the exchanges between sustained upper notes and left-hand semiquavers.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Final bars, descent and ascent
cues.text: The last runs descend from the treble into the low bass, where a note is held under the pedal. The hands then climb again. A high tremolo and a short final chord end the continuous movement.
cues.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Prélude, final page; Piano Practical Editions, bars 91–97, pp. 12–13. https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/48/IMSLP560971-PMLP4975-Le_Tombeau_de_Couperin.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The left hand takes over
transitions.from: A · Semiquavers with ornaments, E minor
transitions.to: Dev · Running notes in the left hand
transitions.how: The second ending carries the E minor opening on into the next section. The semiquavers continue, and the left hand plays them more and more often below sustained notes in the right hand. As the running line moves into the bass, both hands keep the same light articulation.
transitions.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), pp. 3–5: first and second endings and the continuation with left-hand runs.

transitions.title: Descending runs to the bass
transitions.to: Coda · Falling runs and held notes
transitions.how: The descending semiquavers cross between the hands and reach a low note, which is held under the pedal. Ravel keeps that bass sounding while a new arpeggio rises towards the final high tremolo. The running figure continues to the last chord.
transitions.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Prélude, final page; Piano Practical Editions, bars 91–97, pp. 12–13.

composer.epithet: Composer of a ballet built from two tunes and a snare drum, and of a suite of dances dedicated to his war dead.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1889; Fauré for composition, André Gedalge for counterpoint
Ricardo Viñes · Maurice Delage · Tristan Klingsor · M. D. Calvocoressi

Two operas, two piano concertos, ballets, songs, chamber and piano music; no symphony

quote.text: Does it never occur to these people that I may be artificial by nature?
quote.source: To M. D. Calvocoressi, recalled in his Musicians Gallery (1933)

composer.background:
Ravel’s father took his sons to factories to see the machinery, and his mother sang to them. Pierre-Joseph was a Swiss-born engineer; Marie Delouart was Basque and had grown up in Madrid. Maurice was born in Ciboure on 7 March 1875, and the family moved to Paris three months later. He went back to the Basque coast many times. Spain appears often in his music, in the plucked-guitar attacks of Alborada del gracioso, the habanera in the Rapsodie espagnole and the clocks of a Toledo clockmaker’s shop in L’heure espagnole.

He entered the Paris Conservatoire at fourteen, studied piano with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot and lost his place in 1895 for failing to win the required prizes. André Gedalge gave him counterpoint lessons from 1897, and in January 1898 he entered the composition class of Fauré. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, gave the first performances of Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit, pieces he could not have played himself with comparable command.
